pillar_reactions.evidence: Volunteered his own mobility limitation unprompted and tied it straight to a goal the rep had not surfaced: 'I'm not a flexible person, like I cannot touch my toes... in terms of being able to play with my kids when they're older and lots of value in my life, I definitely want to, I need to get more flexible.' He had also asked a mechanics question just before the pillar — 'how clear of a progressive model is it? You know, are there specific workout patterns? Is it progressing?'

'Very willing. This is probably the biggest area.' He went further and diagnosed himself — 'I view food as fun, not as fuel, which I think is what's been hard for me' — and asked for specifics: 'even if it is, you know, down to the specifics of like, here are some potential meals'.

'Yeah, that's great. Yeah, no questions... I think that makes a lot of sense.' He later asked mechanics questions about the delivery rather than the substance — whether the Thursday live sessions were open to all levels, and how many clients Trevor takes: 'he only takes a select few, what is kind of his target number?' He also pre-discounted the headline benefit: 'I probably wouldn't be texting Trevor, you know, when I'm at the grocery store... I love to know he's available, but I probably wouldn't be very demanding.'

anchors.raw: I think I can get a nutrition... And personal trainer for easily under $400 a month. That's local that I can see in person. So yeah, I love that you guys make yourselves available, but it's still not an in-person trainer.
anchors.competitor: Local in-person personal trainer and nutritionist
anchors.note: He is comparing on a per-month basis against in-person delivery and concluding that remote should cost less, not more. The offer's differentiator — one-to-one access to Trevor — is the exact thing he says he would not use.

anchors.raw: I'd probably expect to pay less than $400 a month. Probably around $200 to $300, I'd be all in. But at $1,000, that's probably a no.
anchors.note: A specific band stated unprompted, roughly a fifth of the $1,000/month the flagship works out to. He framed it as a value judgement rather than an affordability limit — 'it's a hard question to answer. You know, obviously your health is worth a lot. I just think I could do it for less.'

anchors.raw: a lot of the things I've done before have been investing in a lot of equipment and things
anchors.note: He has already bought a home gym, calisthenics rig and a new grill. Prior capital outlay is doing double work here: it sets his mental price for solving this problem and it removes the equipment argument the rep leaned on.

anchors.raw: That's $200 a month for two grand a year.
anchors.note: The strongest anchor against the $6,000 was created by the rep himself, four minutes after the price landed. It also matches the number the prospect had just named, so it validates his band rather than the flagship's.

unmet_demand.want: A way for his wife and his 53-year-old father to do some version of the programme alongside him — 'even if my wife in some way could, could do some version of this, or my dad could, I think that would help all of us'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is single-person one-to-one coaching. The rep answered with encouragement to teach them himself — 'take them through it. Why not? That's always good. Grow together' — and never mentioned that a lower-cost community tier exists which would have served exactly this, even though he introduced that tier twenty minutes later for a different reason.

unmet_demand.want: Meaningful one-to-one coaching at roughly $200-300 a month
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The only product at that price drops the one-to-one entirely — 'it is just everything that we just talked about, just minus the one-to-one aspect'. There is nothing between $200/month community and $1,000/month flagship.

unmet_demand.want: Training that is genuinely gamified — targets, scoring and progression he can play against, which he named as the single thing that makes him stick to anything
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He said the word 'gamify' first and the rep echoed it at least six times, but nothing gamified was ever described. What was actually offered was app logging, a weekly check-in, form-video review and a monthly community challenge. The prospect accepted the word without ever being shown the mechanic.
